newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UNHCR-West's troops must not abandon Hutu refugees.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR-West's troops must not abandon Hutu refugees.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency urged Western powers on Tuesday not to abandon plans to deploy a military force in east Zaire, saying troops were needed urgently to reach 500,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees scattered around Bukavu.

"There's a big job for a multinational force to be done in eastern Zaire. Its priority should now be Bukavu where there are still half a million refugees," UNHCR spokeswoman Christiane Berthiaume told a news briefing.
"We need help. This is a huge job. We can't do it on our own."

Many countries have urged a re-think on plans for the Canadian-led multinational task force after 500,000 Hutus returned home from the Goma region, about 100 km (60 miles) northeast of Bukavu, following Tutsi rebel shelling of Mugunga camp that forced Hutu militia to flee.
The United States and South Africa were reluctant volunteers and have seized on the mass migration as a sign that the force should be radically sized down or even scrapped.

But French President Jacques Chirac said during a visit to Japan that Paris still believed multinational intervention was needed. Britain has also said it still expects at least part of the force to be deployed, expressing concern about Bukavu.
Until last week, the focus of relief efforts was on securing humanitarian corridors in eastern Zaire. Now agencies are scrambling to cope with an unprecedented number of returnees.

The Washington Post reported in Tuesday's edition that senior U.S. officials had tentatively concluded that the 10,000 strong force was no longer needed. Canada's Defence Minister Don Young seemed to be edging towards the same view.
Rwanda also says the force is no longer needed because 40 per cent of its refugees in Zaire have returned voluntarily.
But Berthiaume said UNHCR had been denied access to Bukavu by Tutsi rebels who control the area and that the multinational force was needed to open the border and provide access.
She said UNHCR was relieved that refugees in Goma had gone home but the problems were not over yet.

"We've been lucky so far. All has gone quite well. But there are still half a million people out there who need help," she said. "We've been denied access to Bukavu. We're very worried about these people. They haven't got food for almost a month."
The refugees in Bukavu are scattered around a strip 300 km (190 miles) long. Some are known to have walked 200 km (125 miles) westwards, into Zaire's inaccessible interior.
They were caught up in a month-long conflict between the Zairean Tutsi rebels, refugee Hutu extremists and Zaire's army.
Berthiaume said UNHCR had no reports of movement in Bukavu although Western aid sources say some refugees are moving north.
The exodus could pick up again if the rebels, who have close links with Kigali, open a corridor in the Bukavu region so tens of thousands of refugees further south can also go home.
In Goma, Berthiaume said the exodus out of Zaire had slowed down to 1,000 an hour from a peak of 15,000 at the weekend.
She said an estimated 200,000 people, Hutu militia and their families, had fled to the hills near Goma. "We can assume the big majority of these people will not go home," she said.

The Hutus fled in 1994 after Tutsi-led rebels won a civil war and took power in Kigali. The political and military leaders of the defeated Hutu regime were mainly based in Zaire. They and many ordinary refugees took part in 1994's Hutu-led genocide of more than half a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
